title: The Afternoon Brief: Midwest flooding crests; marriage fraud charges; Ukraine strikes Russian grain port
dek: Indiana rivers hit multi-decade highs as the Midwest's fourth day of flooding persists; federal prosecutors charge 11 in a $100 million marriage fraud scheme spanning 1,000+ sham unions; and Ukraine strikes Russia's Novorossiysk grain terminals, threatening global wheat supplies.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Three major stories define the day's scope: a domestic infrastructure crisis from severe weather, a federal prosecution exposing immigration vetting vulnerabilities, and an escalation in the maritime dimension of the Ukraine-Russia conflict with direct commodity-market consequences.
bottom_line: Indiana rivers crested at multi-decade highs as Midwest flooding entered its fourth day, the Justice Department charged 11 people in a $100 million marriage fraud scheme exposing immigration vetting gaps, and Ukraine launched a massive drone and missile strike on Russia's Novorossiysk grain terminals, threatening global wheat supplies. Watch for power restoration timelines and continued flood risk through the coming days, for trial proceedings in the marriage fraud case and the government's process for revoking fraudulent green cards, and for commodity market reactions to the disrupted Russian grain exports and any Russian retaliation against Ukrainian targets.
body: The Midwest's flooding disaster entered its fourth consecutive day Thursday as rivers across Indiana crested at levels unseen in decades. The White River at Muncie was cresting at its highest point in more than 80 years, with forecasters warning it would reach even higher levels downstream at Anderson, its highest in more than 100 years by Thursday evening. More than 250,000 Indiana customers remained without power Thursday morning. Parts of the region absorbed 6 to nearly 12 inches of rain over the week, and at least four rivers in eastern Indiana were forecast to reach major flood stage into Thursday, meaning flooding could persist even after the heaviest rain has stopped. The storm that triggered the flooding killed at least two people across the region early in the week, with confirmed deaths in Jennings County, Indiana and Roseville, Ohio. These figures extend the crisis that began Tuesday with severe weather and tornadoes across Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois that initially left more than 700,000 without power.

In federal court, the Justice Department charged 11 people with orchestrating an extensive marriage fraud scheme involving over 1,000 sham marriages between Chinese nationals and U.S. citizens from 2016 through July 2026. The New York City-based network operated as what Attorney General Todd Blanche called "one of the largest marriage fraud prosecutions in United States history." Foreign nationals paid as much as $100,000 per fraudulent marriage to bypass legal immigration pathways; the operation generated tens of millions of dollars over its decade-long run. The indictment secures no verdicts, trial proceedings remain ahead, but the scale and sophistication of the scheme, operating across professional service networks, exposes unresolved vulnerabilities in the marriage-based green card vetting process. The central unanswered question is how many of the 1,000+ fraudulent marriages resulted in green cards being issued, and what the government's process will be for identifying and revoking them.

Ukraine escalated its maritime campaign against Russian infrastructure Thursday by launching a massive drone and missile barrage on Russia's port of Novorossiysk on the Black Sea, damaging two major grain export terminals and striking the last significant Russian naval base on the Black Sea. The overnight attack killed three people, including an eight-year-old child, and injured 24 others. An emergency situation was declared in Novorossiysk after drones struck port areas and damaged pipelines, suspending the city's water supply. Ukraine's military said four Russian warships, including two frigates, were hit. Moscow-based analytics firms assessed that Russian grain exports for August could fall more than half compared to the same month over the prior five years. Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter; the disruption carries immediate commodity-market implications and signals that each side's targeting of the other's port and grain infrastructure is accelerating. The reporting does not specify which two terminals were struck, their capacity, the timeline for repairs, or current operational status of Ukraine's own export routes.

These three developments, domestic flooding crisis, immigration enforcement action, and maritime escalation in an active war, move through separate channels but share a common characteristic: each tests the government's capacity to manage or respond to complex, large-scale disruptions. The flooding's persistence depends on weather patterns over the next hours; the marriage fraud prosecution's outcome depends on court proceedings; and the grain-infrastructure war's trajectory depends on the two sides' willingness to sustain or escalate further strikes.
